lesson.title: Raising a Power to a Power: Why You Multiply the Exponents
lesson.summary: When an already-exponentiated quantity gets raised to another power, such as (x^3)^4, the exponents multiply instead of add, because you are repeating a group of factors rather than combining two separate groups.
lesson.body:
The power rule for exponents handles expressions like (x^3)^4, where a power is itself raised to another power. It is easy to confuse this with the product rule from a couple lessons back, so it helps to be precise about what (x^3)^4 actually means: it means x^3 multiplied by itself 4 times, since the outer exponent of 4 tells you how many copies of the base x^3 to multiply together. Writing that out, (x^3)^4 = x^3 times x^3 times x^3 times x^3.

Now the product rule for exponents (same base, add the exponents) applies directly to those four copies: x^3 times x^3 times x^3 times x^3 = x^(3+3+3+3) = x^12. Adding 3 four times is the same as multiplying 3 by 4, so this simplifies to x^(3 times 4) = x^12. That is the power rule: (a^m)^n = a^(m times n). Rather than being a separate fact to memorize, it is really the product rule applied repeatedly, which is why it is worth learning the two rules in this order.

A numeric check keeps the two rules from blurring together. Compute (2^2)^3 directly: 2^2 = 4, and then 4^3 = 4 times 4 times 4 = 64. Using the power rule instead, (2^2)^3 = 2^(2 times 3) = 2^6. Since 2^6 = 64 as well, both methods agree.

The rule also applies when a coefficient sits inside the parentheses along with the variable, but each factor inside gets raised to the outer power separately. To simplify (2x^3)^2, raise both the 2 and the x^3 to the power of 2: (2x^3)^2 = 2^2 times (x^3)^2 = 4 times x^(3 times 2) = 4x^6. You can double-check this by expanding directly: (2x^3)^2 = 2x^3 times 2x^3 = (2 times 2) times (x^3 times x^3) = 4 times x^(3+3) = 4x^6, which matches.

Because the power rule multiplies exponents while the product rule adds them, mixing the two up is one of the most common errors in this unit. A useful habit is to ask what operation sits between the two exponent expressions before you touch a single number: if it is multiplication of two separate powers with the same base, like x^3 times x^4, you add exponents; if it is one power sitting inside another, like (x^3)^4, you multiply exponents. Reading the expression carefully before applying a rule will save you from the single most common slip in exponent work.

The power rule also explains what happens when an exponent of 0 sits on the outside, tying back to the very first lesson in this unit. Consider (x^5)^0. Applying the power rule gives x^(5 times 0) = x^0, and the zero exponent rule says x^0 = 1, as long as x is not 0. This matches the direct reasoning too, since any nonzero quantity raised to the power of 0, including the whole quantity x^5, must equal 1. The two rules again agree, which is exactly the kind of consistency that makes it safe to trust these shortcuts instead of re-deriving each one by expansion every time. A slightly longer example shows the power rule combined with the product rule in one simplification. Simplify (3x^2y)^3. The outer exponent of 3 applies to every factor inside the parentheses: the coefficient 3, the x^2, and the y (which carries an invisible exponent of 1). That gives 3^3 times (x^2)^3 times y^(1 times 3) = 27 times x^(2 times 3) times y^3 = 27x^6y^3. You can check the exponent on x by expanding directly: (3x^2y)^3 means three copies of 3x^2y multiplied together, and each copy contributes 2 factors of x, for 3 times 2 = 6 factors of x total, matching x^6.
